books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John Brown, address to the Virginia court (November 2, 1859)

stimulus.source_note: John Brown, address to the Virginia court, November 2, 1859, before sentencing for the Harpers Ferry raid. Public domain. Wording verified against the Gilder Lehrman transcript (Address of John Brown to the Virginia Court, GLC05508.051) and the Dickinson House Divided text. The two passages appear in this order in the address; omissions are marked.
stimulus.text: I never did intend murder, or treason, or the destruction of property, or to excite or incite slaves to rebellion, or to make insurrection. . . . I believe that to have interfered as I have done . . . in behalf of His despised poor, was not wrong, but right.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note

rationales.A: Background from the books: Brown was captured, tried, and hanged on December 2, 1859; escape was never in question.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Northerners called Brown a martyr, and Southerners read that praise as proof that more abolitionist raids were coming.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the Virginia court convicted Brown of treason and hanged him; it did not free him.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Lincoln was not yet president in 1859 and could pardon no one.
rationales.general:
1. Watch the North: Brown’s speech made him a martyr, not a criminal, in Northern eyes.
2. Watch the South: that praise looked like an invitation to the next raid.
3. See the fear: if the North honored a man who seized a federal arsenal, no Southern home was safe.
Remember: a martyr’s speech can frighten the other side more than his raid did.
